provenance.provenance_evidence: The project-owned projection passage reproduces the retained calendar body hash exactly. Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1922 Tours Mame antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: Mame prints alleluja with j where the 1962 prints Alleluia / alleluia with i, and lower-cases the first of the pair inside the parenthesis.; Mame lower-cases regem and regi where the 1962 capitalises Regem and Regi.; Mame closes the Tempore paschali parenthesis before the full stop (... saeculorum (T. P. alleluja, alleluja).); the 1962 sets the stop inside (... saeculorum. (T. P. Alleluia, alleluia.)).. Corroboration: 1862 Pustet page-image collation of 2026-08-26, Pustet printed pp. [53]-[54]; Internet Archive leaves n722-n723 (Pustet coelum retains oe; target caelum uses ae.; Pustet Alleluja uses j; target Alleluia uses i.), outcome collated-non-exact. Two non-exactnesses were recorded against the Pustet: coelum with oe, and the j of Alleluja. THE MAME PRINTS caelum WITH THE AE LIGATURE and so does NOT share the first; it does share the second. The Mame is a French printing that uses j for consonantal i throughout its body text, so its j-forms here are systematic house orthography, not a local variant. On this point the Mame AGREES WITH THE 1862 PUSTET AGAINST THE 1962, so the human review's observation stands on two independent public-domain witnesses, and no public-domain page yet seen authorises the 1962's i-spelling of this word as an exact string..

propers.text:
Salve, sancta parens, enixa puerpera Regem: qui caelum terramque regit in
saecula saeculorum. (T. P. Alleluia, alleluia.) Eructavit cor meum verbum
bonum: dico ego opera mea Regi. V. Gloria Patri.
